title: Transporting back to rides past
author: Prajwal K. Rajesh
content_html:
I can’t remember the last time I heard the cling of an auto fare meter.

As a child, it was a sound I heard almost every day. Before every ride, there would be the usual conversation. The “auto uncle” would say he wanted “one and a half”, which meant you have to pay one-and-a-half times the fare. My mother would argue that it wasn’t a long distance and refuse. After a bit of back and forth, they would usually settle somewhere in the middle.

Only then would the ride begin.

The driver would flip down a small metal lever, almost shaped like a spoon, and the fare meter would make a sharp metallic cling. It was such a small sound, but it meant the journey had officially started. Like the starting bell of a race, it marked the beginning of another ride through the city.

Back then, the fare meter was a chunky metal box with spinning numbers that slowly climbed as the auto moved. It was as much a part of the ride as the wind on your face or the sound of traffic.

Then came digital fare meters. The spinning numbers were replaced with a digital display, but thankfully, the familiar cling stayed. It was one small reminder that some things hadn’t changed.

But even that didn’t last.

With the arrival of ride-hailing apps, fare meters slowly disappeared. The fare was already on your phone before you even stepped into the auto. There was no meter to watch, no lever to pull, and no cling to hear.

Like all things, even “modern” has an expiry date.

Today, the fare meter has almost disappeared, and that metallic cling has become a rare sound. But every now and then, I hear it again, not on the road, but as the notification tone of a ride app.

It’s funny how a simple sound can outlive the thing that created it.

For most people, it’s just another notification. But for those who grew up with auto rides, meter negotiations, and spinning numbers, it’s a tiny reminder of a city that once sounded a little different.
